summary: Specifies a Telnet authentication scheme, under the framework of RFC 2941, using the Secure Remote Password (SRP) mechanism.

eli5.summary: SRP lets you prove you know a password without sending the password. This plugs that trick into Telnet.

questions: how does srp work with telnet
what modulus size does telnet srp need
what is the srp sha1 session key length
subtitle: How Telnet uses the Secure Remote Password protocol so a user can log in without sending a password.

tldr.problem: Telnet logins normally send a password that anyone watching the network can read, and the client and server do not prove anything to each other.
tldr.mechanism: Under the Telnet Authentication Option (RFC 2941), the client and server run the SRP-SHA1 mechanism from RFC 2945 by exchanging parameters, exponential residues and short proofs that each side knows the session key.
tldr.outcome: Only one-way, client-to-server mode is defined. SRP's two-way proofs still give implicit mutual authentication and a 40-byte session key that Telnet encryption can use.

today: RFC 2944 is a Proposed Standard from September 2000. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: SRP Inside the Authentication Option
sections.content:
RFC 2944 plugs the Secure Remote Password (SRP) mechanism into the Telnet Authentication Option from RFC 2941. The specific mechanism is SRP-SHA1, which is described in RFC 2945. This memo only defines how its messages are carried in Telnet sub-options.

The authentication type is SRP, code 5. The sub-option commands are AUTH (0), REJECT (1), ACCEPT (2), CHALLENGE (3), RESPONSE (4), EXP (8) and PARAMS (9).
sections.eli5: SRP is a way to prove you know a password without telling it. This RFC just says which Telnet messages carry the steps.

sections.title: The SRP Sub-option Commands
sections.content:
Each command follows the pattern IAC SB AUTHENTICATION IS|REPLY <authentication-type-pair> <command> ... IAC SE.

  • AUTH (client): the client has supplied the user name and is ready to receive that user's field parameters. It carries no authentication data and should only be sent after the NAME command.
  • PARAMS (server): the three values n (modulus), g (generator) and s (salt).
  • EXP (client): the client's exponential residue, called A.
  • CHALLENGE (server): the server's exponential residue. The RFC describes it as the sum of two residues, g^x + g^b.
  • RESPONSE (client): a 160-bit (20 byte) proof of the client's authenticity.
  • ACCEPT (server): authentication succeeded, with the server's own proof as data.
  • REJECT (server): authentication failed, with an optional ASCII reason.

In PARAMS, each of the three values is preceded by a 16-bit length in network byte order. EXP has no count because it holds one value. CHALLENGE, RESPONSE and ACCEPT have no count because they are fixed in size.
sections.eli5: There are a few kinds of message: hello with my name, here are the numbers to use, here is my answer, here is yours, and finally yes or no.

sections.title: Implementation Rules
sections.content:
Only AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER mode is supported, and only the AUTH_HOW_ONE_WAY mode is defined. SRP's two-way proofs already give implicit mutual authentication. AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL is reserved for an explicit mutual variant to be defined in a future specification.

Large numbers in PARAMS and EXP go in network byte order, most significant byte first, with no padding.

SRP-SHA1 produces a 40-byte session key. Implementations can use different keys for incoming and outgoing traffic, which makes the encrypted session more secure. The RFC recommends that the Telnet ENCRYPT method, if used, be able to take advantage of the longer keys.

If the modifier byte, the second byte of the type pair, has any bits other than AUTH_WHO_MASK or AUTH_HOW_MASK set, both bytes are included in the session key hash. This confirms the type pair was negotiated correctly while staying compatible with existing software.
sections.eli5: The rules say how to write big numbers down, which direction the checking goes, and how to make the secret key long enough to be strong.

sections.title: A Login Walk-through
sections.content:
User tjw wants to log in on machine foo. The server offers SRP CLIENT|ONE_WAY|ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT and falls back to SRP CLIENT|ONE_WAY if the client cannot do encryption. The client sends NAME and then AUTH. The server looks up the field and salt for the user in its password file and sends PARAMS.

The client prompts the user for the password. The two sides swap exponential residues with EXP and CHALLENGE and compute their session keys. The client then sends RESPONSE, the message M that proves it holds the session key. If ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT was agreed, the two octets of the type pair are appended to the session key K before the hash for M is computed. Otherwise nothing is appended.

The response and the server's proof are as long as the hash output, which is 20 bytes for SHA-1. The server answers with ACCEPT and its own proof, or with REJECT.
sections.eli5: You tell the computer your name, it sends some numbers, you type your password into your own computer only, and you each send a proof you did the math right.

sections.title: Negotiation Risks and Modulus Size
sections.content:
Negotiating a mechanism should be used with caution. During negotiation, no authentication has happened yet, so neither side knows whether it is talking to the system it intends. An intruder could try to push the use of an authentication system that is weak or already compromised.

SRP relies on the security of the underlying public-key cryptosystem, so the modulus n should be large enough to resist brute-force attack. The RFC recommends at least 1024 bits. Implementations should reject moduli shorter than 512 bits and invalid moduli or generators, meaning a non-safe-prime n or a non-primitive g.
sections.eli5: Before you agree on a lock, a bad guy could try to talk you into a flimsy one. And the secret numbers must be big enough that nobody can guess them.
